questions.q: Why does the serialized input include both the original messy record and the candidate, rather than just the candidate alone?
options: Because DistilBERT requires exactly two sentences as input
Because the model's job is to judge the candidate relative to what it started from, which requires seeing the original
Because the tokenizer cannot process a single record
Because including both halves the training time
questions.explain: A candidate that looks clean in isolation but silently dropped information from the original is exactly the case this project needs the model to catch, which requires seeing both in the same input.

questions.q: What model architecture does the reward model use?
options: A random forest over hand-engineered features
distilbert-base-uncased plus a scalar linear head on the pooled output
A full GPT-style decoder with a classification head
A convolutional network over character embeddings
questions.explain: The reward model fine-tunes distilbert-base-uncased and adds a linear layer that outputs a single scalar score from the pooled representation.

questions.q: What is the pairwise Bradley-Terry / logistic loss used to train this model?
options: Mean squared error between r_chosen and a fixed target of 1.0
-log(sigmoid(r_chosen - r_rejected))
Cross-entropy between the candidate text and the original text
A simple accuracy metric used directly as the loss
questions.explain: The loss pushes the margin between the chosen and rejected scores to be positive, without ever requiring an absolute target value.

questions.q: Why does training use only a few epochs and a small batch size on this dataset?
options: Because distilbert-base-uncased cannot process batches larger than 8
Because with only roughly 260 pairs, more epochs would risk overfitting to one rater's idiosyncrasies rather than the general pattern
Because AdamW does not support more than 4 epochs
Because GPU memory cannot hold more than 8 examples
questions.explain: A small dataset trained for too many epochs risks memorizing specific rater quirks instead of learning generalizable preference patterns.

questions.q: How does this reward model differ fundamentally from Project 3's reward signal?
options: They are the same model, reused across both projects
This is a genuinely separate learned model trained on human pairwise preferences; Project 3's reward is a programmatic execution-correctness check with no learned component
Project 3's reward is also trained with a Bradley-Terry loss on human preferences
This reward model has no training data at all
questions.explain: Project 2 trains an actual neural network on human preference labels, while Project 3 computes its reward by running SQL and comparing result sets — no learning involved.
